# Why don`t we use extremely thin oils in engines

Viscosity is often treated as a simple number on an oil bottle, but it represents a fundamental trade-off between fluid dynamics and mechanical protection. While lower viscosity oils indeed offer superior flow characteristicsâreducing pump work and allowing for faster oil-to-metal contact at cold startsâthey introduce significant risks when pushed to the extreme of "extremely thin" grades. The decision to avoid ultra-low viscosity oils in high-performance or heavy-duty applications isn't just about cost; it is a matter of thermodynamic limits, tribological failure modes, and system architecture.

The most immediate consequence of drastically reducing oil viscosity is the collapse of the elastohydrodynamic lubrication (EHL) film thickness. In an engine bearing, the oil must maintain a specific minimum film thickness to separate moving surfaces. If this film becomes too thin, we transition from boundary lubrication to mixed or direct metal-to-metal contact. Even though thinner oil improves volumetric efficiency by reducing leakage past piston ringsâa primary source of blow-by and hydrocarbon emissionsâthe loss of load-carrying capacity is unacceptable under high combustion pressures.

Consider the crankshaft main bearing. At operating temperature, the engine generates immense shear forces. Extremely thin oils possess lower film strength, meaning they are more susceptible to cavitation and starvation in high-load zones. When the oil film ruptures, metal asperities weld together momentarily, leading to scuffing or seizure. This is not merely a matter of "wear"; it is catastrophic failure. The source material correctly identifies that while thin oils facilitate better precision in parts measurements due to reduced clearance issues, this benefit vanishes instantly if the lubrication regime shifts from hydrodynamic to boundary.

Thermal stability is another critical factor. Lower viscosity oils generally have lower flash points and are more prone to thermal oxidation at high temperatures. In a modern turbocharged engine, oil temperatures can exceed 120Â°C in the piston crown area. Extremely thin oils lack the molecular structure necessary to resist breaking down under these shear and heat loads. Once an oil oxidizes, it forms sludge and varnish, which clogs oil galleries. A thinner base oil provides less resistance to this degradation, effectively creating a faster feedback loop between thermal stress and viscosity breakdown.

Contamination resistance is equally problematic. Oil acts as a suspension medium for soot, metal wear particles, and combustion byproducts. Thicker oils have higher yield stresses, allowing them to trap these contaminants and transport them away from critical surfaces until an oil change occurs. Extremely thin oils have negligible yield stress; they allow contaminants to pass directly through the filter media or settle on bearing journals. Furthermore, because there is less bulk oil volume to dilute the concentration of particulates, a thin film becomes instantly contaminated with abrasive debris, accelerating the wear rate exponentially.

From a manufacturing standpoint, producing extremely thin oils with extreme pressure (EP) additives that remain effective at such low viscosities is chemically difficult. You cannot simply add more thickener; you need to engineer the base oil and additive package to maintain film integrity without increasing drag. This drives up production costs significantly, making the product economically unviable for mass-market engines where reliability margins are tight.

In software architecture, we often face similar trade-offs between performance metrics and system stability. Optimizing for raw speed (low viscosity) without accounting for load handling (film strength) leads to a system that crashes under stress. Similarly, in engine design, selecting an oil grade is not just about minimizing friction; it is about ensuring the lubrication film survives the worst-case operating scenario.

For developers working on embedded systems or simulation models, this principle applies directly to fluid dynamics solvers. When modeling internal combustion engines, assuming a linear relationship between viscosity reduction and efficiency gain ignores the non-linear failure modes introduced by film collapse. The code must account for the transition point where hydrodynamic lift fails, not just the drag reduction benefits.

Ultimately, the industry standard exists because it balances these competing forces. We do not use extremely thin oils because the marginal gain in fuel economy or startup precision is outweighed by the exponential increase in failure probability under thermal and load stress.
